title: About RepAdapt
text:
The RepAdapt project aims to learn about the flexibility of adaptation: if different species encounter a similar adaptive challenge, do they use the same genes to adapt? By comparing genome sequence data from thousands of individuals across hundreds of species, we can search for signatures of natural selection within each species and explore the diversity of responses across species. In the early stages of this project, we are focusing on adaptation to climate, and will eventually expand the scope to other selection pressures and traits. Given the importance for crop breeding, we are also particularly interested in comparisons between wild and domestic species. With the recent launch of the MacroMar project, which will greatly expand the number of marine species, we will also explore how changes in the marine environment have driven adaptive responses.
The RepAdapt project began with a study of the genetic basis of repeated adaptation to climate in 25 species of plants. After using Genotype-Environment Association (GEA) methods and finding many genes with significant signatures of repeated local adaptation (Whiting et al. 2024), we next looked at patterns of repeated selective sweeps (Nocchi et al. 2024). Surprisingly, whereas the genes driving local adaptation were enriched for high pleiotropy, the candidates driving global adaptation were enriched for low pleiotropy. This pattern is consistent with expectations from migration-selection theory (Yeaman 2022), where local adaptation should be enriched for alleles of large effect. Given that high pleiotropy tends to involve large phenotypic effects (Wang et al. 2010), seeing genes with high pleiotropy driving local adaptation is consistent with this broad prediction.

What other predictions from evolutionary theory can we test using comparative population genomics? Ultimately, we would like to learn how constraints in the genotype-phenotype-fitness map give rise to repeated adaptation (Yeaman et al. 2018). To learn about such constraints, we can compare the extent of repeated adaptation for:
By using a common set of methods to call variants and analyze patterns of genomic variation for signatures of selection, we will have an unprecedented scale at which to study the comparative population genomics of adaptation.

title: Publications
section: The genetic architecture of repeated local adaptation to climate in distantly related plants, Whiting, J.R., Booker, T.R., Rougeux, C. et al., 2024
text:
The genetic architecture of repeated local adaptation to climate in distantly related plants, Whiting, J.R., Booker, T.R., Rougeux, C. et al., 2024


Abstract

Closely related species often use the same genes to adapt to similar environments. However, we know little about why such genes possess increased adaptive potential and whether this is conserved across deeper evolutionary lineages. Adaptation to climate presents a natural laboratory to test these ideas, as even distantly related species must contend with similar stresses. Here, we re-analyse genomic data from thousands of individuals from 25 plant species as diverged as lodgepole pine and Arabidopsis (~300 Myr). We test for genetic repeatability based on within-species associations between allele frequencies in genes and variation in 21 climate variables. Our results demonstrate significant statistical evidence for genetic repeatability across deep time that is not expected under randomness, identifying a suite of 108 gene families (orthogroups) and gene functions that repeatedly drive local adaptation to climate. This set includes many orthogroups with well-known functions in abiotic stress response. Using gene co-expression networks to quantify pleiotropy, we find that orthogroups with stronger evidence for repeatability exhibit greater network centrality and broader expression across tissues (higher pleiotropy), contrary to the ‘cost of complexity’ theory. These gene families may be important in helping wild and crop species cope with future climate change, representing important candidates for future study.

title: Publications
section: Repeated global adaptation across plant species, G. Nocchi,J.R. Whiting, & S. Yeaman, 2024
text:
Repeated global adaptation across plant species, G. Nocchi,J.R. Whiting, & S. Yeaman, 2024


Abstract

Global adaptation occurs when all populations of a species undergo selection toward a common optimum. This can occur by a hard selective sweep with the emergence of a new globally advantageous allele that spreads throughout a species’ natural range until reaching fixation. This evolutionary process leaves a temporary trace in the region affected, which is detectable using population genomic methods. While selective sweeps have been identified in many species, there have been few comparative and systematic studies of the genes involved in global adaptation. Building upon recent findings showing repeated genetic basis of local adaptation across independent populations and species, we asked whether certain genes play a more significant role in driving global adaptation across plant species. To address this question, we scanned the genomes of 17 plant species to identify signals of repeated global selective sweeps. Despite the substantial evolutionary distance between the species analyzed, we identified several gene families with strong evidence of repeated positive selection. These gene families tend to be enriched for reduced pleiotropy, consistent with predictions from Fisher’s evolutionary model and the cost of complexity hypothesis. We also found that genes with repeated sweeps exhibit elevated levels of gene duplication. Our findings contrast with recent observations of increased pleiotropy in genes driving local adaptation, consistent with predictions based on the theory of migration-selection balance.

title: Publications
section: The WZA: A window-based method for characterizing genotype–environment associations., Booker, T. R., Yeaman, S., Whiting, J. R., & Whitlock, M. C., 2024
text:
The WZA: A window-based method for characterizing genotype–environment associations., Booker, T. R., Yeaman, S., Whiting, J. R., & Whitlock, M. C., 2024


Abstract

Genotype–environment association (GEA) studies have the potential to identify the genetic basis of local adaptation in natural populations. Specifically, GEA approaches look for a correlation between allele frequencies and putatively selective features of the environment. Genetic markers with extreme evidence of correlation with the environment are presumed to be tagging the location of alleles that contribute to local adaptation. In this study, we propose a new method for GEA studies called the Weighted-Z Analysis (WZA) that combines information from closely linked sites into analysis windows in a way that was inspired by methods for calculating FST. Performing GEA methods in analysis windows has the advantage that it takes advantage of the increased linkage disequilibrium expected surrounding sites subject to local adaptation. We analyse simulations modelling local adaptation to heterogeneous environments to compare the WZA with existing methods. In the majority of cases we tested, the WZA either outperformed single-SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism)-based approaches or performed similarly. In particular, the WZA outperformed individual SNP approaches when a small number of individuals or demes were sampled. Particularly troubling, we found that some GEA methods exhibit very high false positive rates. We applied the WZA to previously published data from lodgepole pine and identified candidate loci that were identified in the original study alongside numerous loci that were not found in the original study.

title: Publications
section: Using genome scans to identify genes used repeatedly for adaptation, Tom R Booker, Sam Yeaman, Michael C Whitlock, 2023
text:
Using genome scans to identify genes used repeatedly for adaptation, Tom R Booker, Sam Yeaman, Michael C Whitlock, 2023


Abstract

Adaptation occurring in similar genes or genomic regions in distinct lineages provides evolutionary biologists with a glimpse at the fundamental opportunities for and constraints to diversification. With the widespread availability of high-throughput sequencing technologies and the development of population genetic methods to identify the genetic basis of adaptation, studies have begun to compare the evidence for adaptation at the molecular level among distinct lineages. However, methods to study repeated adaptation are often oriented toward genome-wide testing to identify a set of genes with signatures of repeated use, rather than evaluating the significance at the level of an individual gene. In this study, we propose PicMin, a novel statistical method derived from the theory of order statistics that can test for repeated molecular evolution to estimate significance at the level of an individual gene, using the results of genome scans. This method is generalizable to any number of lineages and, indeed, statistical power to detect repeated adaptation increases with the number of lineages that have signals of repeated adaptation of a given gene in multiple lineages.

title: Additional Info
text:
Even distantly related species encounter similar ecological challenges, from climate change to ocean acidification. When presented with the same biological problem, do different species adapt via similar genetic solutions, or does each species evolve a novel response?1,2 As the answer depends critically on the interplay between ecology and genetics3–6, exploring this question will inform our understanding of the universal processes of evolution at a fundamental level. Charting the genetic basis of adaptation also has wide ranging applications, from identifying novel targets for functional genomics in medicine and crop breeding7 to improving conservation management to anticipate climate change8.
Answering this fundamental and longstanding question requires studying many species exposed to the same stress (e.g., climatic variation) and asking how often the same genes recurrently underlie adaptation across lineages. However, progress has been limited in scope: studies of many species commonly examine only a single individual from each (i.e. phylogenetic methods9), whereas studies of many individuals commonly focus on only a single species (i.e. population genomics10). Both approaches miss key signals9,10. Now, new methods and the dramatic growth of genomic datasets enable the simultaneous comparison of many individuals across many species. Recent applications of these methods reveal repeated involvement of specific genes in driving adaptation to climate, even across distantly related species separated by >100M years of evolution11–13. Enabled by new methods developed by our team members14,15, our initial analysis of 25 species found that the spatial patterning of selection influences which genes are repeatedly involved in adaptation across species16,17, consistent with theoretical predictions5. These results show that repeated adaptation is detectable across deep evolutionary timescales, opening a new frontier of scientific inquiry.
Our vision is to push back this frontier, providing unprecedented insights into how adaptation works by making comparisons across hundreds of thousands of individuals from hundreds of species of plants, animals, and fungi. Our systematic cross-species comparisons of genomic responses – unprecedented in breadth – will let us test a wide range of hypotheses about adaptation. This approach will reveal how evolutionary processes interact to shape the architecture of adaptation, and how outcomes vary with phylogenetic grouping, genomic properties, or the type of ecological stress. We envision that an understanding of general principles in ecology and evolution will arise from this coordinated synthesis of datasets across taxa and environments – an effort that requires international, interdisciplinary collaboration.
The RepAdapt working group was formed in September 2024 to tackle this problem, with >100 scientists from 18 countries contributing >300 species datasets with >112,000 individual sequenced samples (Figure 1). The group has developed a set of shared, open bioinformatic workflows (github.com/RepAdapt) and are re-analyzing their datasets using this unified framework. Over the next 5 years, contingent on securing funding, the RepAdapt project will: A) expand and process all suitable species datasets; B) quantify repeatability across species by comparing genomic signatures of adaptation at multiple phylogenetic scales; C) test evolutionary hypotheses about why repeated adaptation varies (as per 5,18,19), and explore the importance of factors such as phylogenetic distance20, pleiotropy21, structural variants22, and the contribution of coding vs. regulatory regions23,24; and D) contextualize what we learn about repeated adaptation by quantifying the proportion of adaptation that is non-repeated using focused studies in several model species, linking genotype, phenotype, and fitness with additional sequencing of existing samples from reciprocal transplant experiments and Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS).

title: Results
text: The foundation of the RepAdapt idea comes from two papers published in 2024, looking at repeatability when it comes to local vs global adaptation. These analyses were done with a much smaller dataset than what we have access to now, but they provide a good starting point for futher analysis.

title: Results
section: The genetic architecture of repeated local adaptation to climate in distantly related plants. (Whitting et al. 2024)
text:
The genetic architecture of repeated local adaptation to climate in distantly related plants. (Whitting et al. 2024)











NoteFigure 1.





a, Sampling locations from all 29 datasets (25 species) and global annual mean temperature. b, An example of six bioclim variables across a single dataset with ten sampling locations from ref. 65. c, An example for the same dataset showing how climate change variables were calculated, taking monthly climate data from the 1960s and 2010s and calculating the effect size of the difference between decades. d, The species tree derived from the OrthoFinder2 analysis for the 17 reference genomes used in this study; species where a reference genome assembly was used to map related species but that species was not included in analyses, are marked with asterisks. The reference genome assembly at each tip came from the species not listed in brackets and species listed in brackets below had their data mapped onto that reference genome. The age of high-confidence nodes is shown with values pulled from TimeTree (Extended Data Fig. 1). Species analysed here are placed according to the reference genome used and the reference’s position in the tree. e,f, The per genome distribution of the number of paralogues per orthogroup (e) and number of representative genomes per orthogroup (f) are depicted as stacked bars, with bar fill scaling from light-to-dark according to most- to least-statistically tractable value. Bars are ordered vertically in line with the tree in d. Ma, million years ago.



Data used in the analysis was sequenced using multiple methods (whole-genome sequencing, capture-based sequencing or pool-sequencing) but all the reads were passed through a common pipeline to pull out single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). This use of a common pipeline minimizes the influence of bioinformatic technical artifacts, therefore reducing the total amount of noise present during analysis. Orthogroups were reconstructed using Orthofinder2 to allow for comparison between different species. The resulting orthogroups had both low rates of paralogy, allowing for reduced confounding effects as well as high presence among species, making detection of repeatability easier. The genes with signatures of local adaptation were then determined by testing the association between allele frequencies and the 21 bioclim variables chosen for the study. SNP p-values were combined into gene p-values using weighted-Z analysis to increase power and reduce error. Finally PicMin was used to identify orthogroups with repeated signatures of association across several species.












NoteFigure 3.





a,b, Heatmaps show the contribution of individual species to orthogroup repeatability at FDR < 0.5 for different climate variables (a) and among pairs of species (b), with species ordered phylogenetically. In each case, the fill of each cell represents the proportion of orthogroups where a given species contributes towards the signature of repeatability based on its minimum GEA P value. c, Heatmap showing the number of times a species contributes towards repeatability for a given RAO (FDR < 0.5). In c, cell fill denotes the number of climate variables where a species contributes a low P value to a given RAO, with grey being 0. The vertical green line separates gymnosperms and angiosperms. Row-wise summations are shown as bars, where the blue bar shows the number of species associated with a given orthogroup (species n) and the red bar shows the total number of species and climate variables (total n). RAOs associated with a single climate variable only have a blue bar and those with stacked red bars are RAOs associated with multiple climate variables. The strongest statistical support for repeatability is also shown per orthogroup as −log10-transformed FDR. Only 73 RAOs with at least five contributing species are shown.



This analysis found 141 repeatedly associated orthogroups (RAOs) with 108 of them unique. It also found that no specific/cluster of species was driving the repeatability signals discovered. Significant orthogroups were also not driven by relatedness between species, showing that the signal of repeatability is spread out across the phylogenetic tree, going against expectations that repeatability is associated with relatedness, declining as relatedness decreases.

title: Results
section: Repeated global adaptation across plant species. (Nocci et al. 2024)
text:
Repeated global adaptation across plant species. (Nocci et al. 2024)











NoteFigure 1.





Geographical distribution and relatedness within and among the study species. (A) Sampling locations of the 17 datasets included in the study. (B)Time-calibrated phylogenetic tree (retrieved from https://timetree.org/) of the 17 datasets, based on 12 reference species. (C) fastSTRUCTURE ancestry pie plot(K = 5) of the Helianthus argophyllus dataset in Texas (USA), showing substantial substructuring. (D) Relatedness filtering summary bar plot by dataset. Datasets labeled by corresponding color from B.



The global adaptation analysis has less species included due to the necessity of whole-genome sequencing for the analysis. However, geographical breadth is largely the same between the two studies and the same bioinformatics pipeline was largely used to allow for accurate comparison.












NoteFigure 3.





Evidence for repeated selectivesweeps across multiple species. (A)Distribution of PicMin FDR (−log10PicMin FDR on the Y axis) for the13,268 tested orthogroups, orderedby number of putative driving geneson the X axis (number of OmegaPlusemp-P < 0.1). Points above the redline have FDR < 0.1. (B) Speciescontribution to PicMin top candidates(FDR < 0.1), calculated for each speciesas: [number of empirical P-values < 0.1in the PicMin FDR < 0.1 orthogroups]/[total number of orthogroups withPicMin FDR < 0.1 tested]. (C) Heatmapof OmegaPlus empirical P-values for the33 candidate orthogroups (PicMin FDR< 0.1); driving genes cells (emp-P < 0.1 –black cells) are outlined in red, speciesare ordered by phylogenetic distancealong the Y axis. A white cell indicatesthat an orthogroup was not tested ina species.





These two studies interestingly display a difference in polygenic genes when looking at local vs global adaptation. In local adaptation polygenic genes are favored for repeatability as their large effect allows them to overcome swamping from migration. In contrast polygenic genes are disfavored in global adaptation due to the cost of complexity hypothesis, wherein mutations to more polygenic genes will possibly cause detrimental impact to a larger number of biological processes.
